title: Sherlock and the Valid String
directAnswer: Reduce the string to two layers of counts. Layer one: how often each letter appears (the frequency map). Layer two: how many letters share each frequency (the frequency-of-frequencies). The string is valid if there is a single distinct frequency, or two distinct frequencies that one deletion can merge — that is, the lower frequency is 1 held by a single letter (delete it whole), or the higher frequency is exactly one above the rest and held by a single letter (delete one of its copies). Everything else is invalid. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.formula:
freq = Counter(s)
ffreq = Counter(freq.values())
valid = (
  len(ffreq) == 1
  or (len(ffreq) == 2 and (
        (lo == 1 and ffreq[lo] == 1)
     or (hi - lo == 1 and ffreq[hi] == 1)))
)
rules: Count the letters, then count those counts — the answer lives in the second layer.
Already uniform (one distinct frequency) ⇒ valid with no deletion.
Two distinct frequencies are repairable only in two precise shapes; everything else is not.
The deletion budget is **one character total**, not one per letter.
Three or more distinct frequencies can never be made equal with a single deletion.
whenToUse: Decide validity when frequencies must match after removing at most one character
The single edit is a deletion (lowers one letter's count by one)
Fixed lowercase alphabet keeps both count maps O(1)
Goal phrased as 'all characters appear the same number of times'
antiSignals: More than one deletion allowed → generalised k-deletion feasibility
Edit is a replacement → frequency-difference (Anagram) reasoning
Need minimum deletions, not yes/no → sum the surpluses instead
Need to report which character to remove → track the offending letter
remember.takeaway: Collapse the frequency map into a frequency-of-frequencies. Because one deletion moves exactly one letter's count by exactly one, a valid string is locked to at most two frequency values separated by a single, single-occurrence step.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you find the two-level count and then enumerate precisely the cases a single deletion can fix, instead of brute-forcing deletions or hand-waving the edge cases.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Applying the one-deletion allowance to several letters at once, missing that three distinct frequencies are unfixable, or requiring only the frequency gap without checking it occurs exactly once.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with the invariant — 'a deletion shifts one letter's count down by one' — then derive that valid strings have ≤ 2 distinct frequencies with a single-step, single-occurrence gap, and name the two repair shapes explicitly.

problemStatement:
Watson asks Sherlock whether a string `s` is **valid**. A string is valid when **all characters appear the same number of times**. It is *also* valid when removing **just one character at one index** leaves every remaining character appearing the same number of times.

Return `"YES"` if `s` is valid and `"NO"` otherwise.
constraints: s contains lowercase English letters only
At most one character may be removed (zero or one)
understanding: Validity is a statement about counts, so we count twice. The first count gives each letter's frequency. The second count groups letters by shared frequency. If they all already share one frequency the string is valid; otherwise a single deletion — which lowers exactly one letter's count by one, possibly to zero — must be enough to make every surviving letter agree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must I always remove a character, or only if needed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only if needed. An already-uniform string is valid with zero deletions; 'just one character' is the cap, not a requirement.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the single edit a deletion or a substitution?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A deletion at one index. It decreases exactly one letter's frequency by one (to zero if that letter appeared once).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the one deletion be spread across two letters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — it is one deletion of one character, affecting a single letter's count.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What alphabet should I assume?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase a–z, so the frequency map and the frequency-of-frequencies map are both bounded by 26 — O(1) space.

examples.explanation: Frequencies a:1, b:1, c:1 → one distinct frequency → already uniform, valid with no deletion.
Frequencies a:1, b:1, c:2 → counts {1:2, 2:1}. The higher frequency 2 is one above 1 and held by a single letter 'c' → delete one 'c' → all counts 1.
Frequencies a:2, b:2, c:1, d:1 → counts {2:2, 1:2}. Two letters sit at count 1; one deletion can rescue only one of them.
Every letter appears 4 times → one distinct frequency → valid as-is.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Delete Every Index and Re-check
approaches.whenToMention: Use it to anchor correctness, then point out that re-counting after each deletion is the avoidable cost.
hints: The definition is an operation: 'remove one character and check uniformity'. What's the most literal way to test it?
Check the original string first; if not uniform, delete each index in turn and re-test uniformity.
Re-counting for all n deletions is O(n) apiece → O(n²). But each deletion is just decrementing one letter's count, so you can decide it from the original counts.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A uniformity check over the 26-letter map is O(n). Trying all n single-character deletions and re-checking is O(n²). The fixed alphabet keeps space O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Start by testing `s` as-is: if all non-zero letter counts are equal, it's valid. Otherwise, for each index `i`, conceptually delete `s[i]`, rebuild the frequency map for the shortened string, and test uniformity. Return `"YES"` at the first deletion that yields uniform counts.

**Why it's the obvious first cut.** The statement is operational — 'remove one character and check' — so the direct simulation removes each character and checks. It's correct beyond doubt.

**Why it's slow.** Recounting the full string after each of `n` deletions repeats nearly identical work `n` times. For `n = 10⁵`, that's ten billion operations.

**Bridge to optimal.** A deletion is fully captured by 'decrement one letter's frequency by one'. So all `n` deletions are knowable from the original frequency map — no string rebuilding required, which leads straight to the frequency-of-frequencies test.
approaches.insight: Because each candidate deletion only nudges one frequency down by one, you can evaluate every possible deletion from the original counts. That observation is what lets the optimal solution skip simulation entirely.

pitfalls: Rebuilding the frequency map for every deletion — O(n²).
Counting zero-frequency letters as breaking uniformity.
Skipping the zero-deletion check, so already-valid strings fall through.

approaches.name: Frequency-of-Frequencies Test (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — 'count letters, count those counts, then test the two repair shapes'.
hints: A single deletion shifts exactly one letter's count by one. How many distinct frequency values can survive that?
Build freq, then ffreq = how many letters have each frequency. One distinct frequency ⇒ valid.
With two distinct frequencies lo < hi: valid only if lo == 1 with a single occurrence (delete that letter whole), or hi == lo + 1 with a single occurrence (delete one of its copies). Otherwise NO.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One O(n) pass builds the frequency map; the rest is constant work over at most 26 frequency values. Both maps are alphabet-bounded → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Count letters into `freq`, then count those frequencies into `ffreq`, a map from 'a frequency value' to 'how many letters have it'. The size of `ffreq` drives the decision.

**One distinct frequency → valid.** All letters already appear equally often; no deletion required.

**Three or more distinct frequencies → invalid.** A single deletion lowers exactly one letter's count by exactly one. It can reconcile at most two frequency groups, never three. Return `"NO"`.

**Exactly two distinct frequencies `lo < hi` — two repair shapes:**

1. **`lo == 1` and a single letter has it.** That letter occurs once; deleting it removes the letter entirely (count 1 → 0) and every survivor shares `hi`. Example: `"aaabbbc"` → counts `{3:2, 1:1}` → delete `c`.

2. **`hi == lo + 1` and a single letter has `hi`.** One letter overshoots by exactly one occurrence; delete one copy (count `hi → lo`) and all letters share `lo`. Example: `"abcc"` → counts `{1:2, 2:1}` → delete one `c`.

Every other two-frequency configuration — two letters tied at count 1 (`"aabbcd"`), or a gap greater than one — requires more than one deletion, so it's `"NO"`.

**Why O(1) space.** Both maps hold at most 26 entries no matter how long `s` is.
approaches.insight: The decisive move is the second count. The first layer exposes each letter's frequency; counting those frequencies reveals whether one deletion can pull everything into agreement. The single-occurrence requirement (`ffreq[lo] == 1` or `ffreq[hi] == 1`) is what stops you from claiming a fix that would actually need several deletions.

Shape 1: a single letter appears once — delete it whole.
Shape 2: a single letter is exactly one too high — delete one copy.

python.explanation: Second-level count of how many letters hold each frequency.
Single distinct frequency ⇒ valid with no deletion.
Two distinct frequency keys, low and high.
Exactly one letter appears once — drop it; the rest already match hi.

diagrams.title: Two-level counting on "abcc"
diagrams.caption: Counts collapse to {1:2, 2:1} — one letter one-too-high, fixable by a single deletion.

edgeCases.behavior: ffreq {3:2, 1:1} → lo==1 and ffreq[lo]==1 → delete lone 'c' → "YES".
ffreq {2:2, 1:2} → two lone letters, neither shape holds → "NO".
ffreq {5:1, 4:1} → hi-lo==1 and ffreq[hi]==1 → delete one 'a' → "YES".

pitfalls: Spending the single deletion across multiple letters.
Forgetting the three-or-more distinct frequencies → always invalid rule.
Checking only the frequency gap without requiring it to occur exactly once.
Confusing shape 1 (lone count-1 letter) with shape 2 (one-too-high letter).

commonMistakes: Applying the single deletion to more than one letter.
Missing that three or more distinct frequencies can never be repaired.
Omitting the single-occurrence requirement on the offending frequency.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Spreading the deletion across letters
commonMistakesDetailed.why: "aabbcd" has two count-1 letters; equalising needs two deletions, but only one is allowed, so it is NO.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# wrong: drops all count-1 letters as if each were free
return "YES" if len({v for v in freq.values() if v > 1}) <= 1 else "NO"
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if len(ffreq) == 2:
    lo, hi = sorted(ffreq)
    if lo == 1 and ffreq[lo] == 1: return "YES"
    if hi - lo == 1 and ffreq[hi] == 1: return "YES"

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the three-frequency case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A single deletion moves one letter by one step and cannot reconcile three distinct frequencies, so ffreq.size() >= 3 is always NO.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dropping the single-occurrence guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: hi == lo + 1 isn't sufficient; if two letters share hi, one deletion fixes only one. The offending frequency must occur exactly once.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if hi - lo == 1 and ffreq[hi] == 1:
    return "YES"

patternNote: Frequency of frequencies (two-level counting). When validity hinges on how character counts may differ under a limited number of edits, count the letters and then count those counts. The frequency-of-frequencies map makes the handful of single-edit-repairable shapes explicit.
